newsitem.title: SPAIN: Drought to shrivel Spain's 1997 durum wheat crop.
newsitem.headline: Drought to shrivel Spain's 1997 durum wheat crop.

text.p: Spain's cereal crop could fall 15 percent from last year's harvest to around 16-17 million tonnes this year after continued weather problems, traders and agricultural experts said on Monday.
Last week's nationwide rain after some months of extremely dry weather has helped to limit some of the damage, but it may still be early for traders to see any price weakening.
"One thing's for sure, prices aren't going to rise any further this week. But they may not fall until Wednesday or so. It depends what suppliers decide to do," said a Barcelona trader.
Some farmers have been hoarding crop stores in anticipation of higher prices, he said.
The recent rainfall may have saved some of the crop, but overall Spanish cereal tonnage will be reduced by roughly 15 percent this year, he said.
"Damage that has been done before the rain arrived can't be recovered now," he said.

Rains resumed last Thursday and continued over the weekend, although the effect on parched crops in the south has been minimal. The crop had already been hit by poor weather late last year, when floods reduced the amount of land sown.

Nationwide, prices were slightly lower today, coming down off last week's highs in all cases except durum wheat. Ex-farm feed wheat prices were at around 26,500 pesetas from 27,000 per tonne, milling wheat was at 27,500 pesetas, barley was at 23,500-23,000 per tonne, while maize was at 24,500.
Durum wheat is static at around 32,000 pesetas per tonne amid limited supply in the south where hard wheat is primarily grown.
"The durum wheat harvest is sure to be sapped by the dry weather, and may be up to 40 percent less than last year," said one Madrid trader.
Last year's Spain's national durum wheat crop was 1.7 million tonnes, of which Andalusia produced around 1.4 tonnes, according to the latest Agriculture Ministry figures.
Farmers association ASAJA estimates last year's durum crop for the region was lower, around 1.26 million tonnes. The group expects this year's harvest to be around 800,000 tonnes.
"The rain's done us good, but it's arrived too late," ASAJA spokesman Jose Vazquez told Reuters.
He estimated that yields this year will be around two tonnes per hectare in the region, versus 2.4 last year and 3.5 in an average year.
Soft wheat for the Andalusia region is forecast at 200,000 tonnes, roughly half last year's figure, although Spain's soft wheat production is concentrated in the Castilla-Leon central region.
"This year has not been typical. First we had floods and then we had the driest March in the century," Vazquez said.
In terms of crop quality, it was still early to say whether cereals will be affected sharply by the climate changes.
"There's no reason why the quality should be bad in particular, but it's early days yet," he said.
